Harodite
HAR-o-dite
n. (the designation of Shammah and Elika, two of David's thirty; named twice)
A gentilic, Hebrew Charodi, presumably from Harod, the spring where Gideon's army was sifted; used twice in one verse, 2 Samuel 23:25.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Harodite stands twice in a single verse of the roll of the thirty: “Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite” (2 Samuel 23:25). Two men of one town were counted among David's mighty men, which is a small honour to a small place. The town is presumably that of the well of Harod, beside which Gideon's thirty-two thousand were reduced to three hundred. The Chronicles parallel gives the form Harorite and a slightly different name, and its margin notes both: “Shammoth the Harorite, Helez the Pelonite” (1 Chronicles 11:27). The verse before in Samuel sets the company: “Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty; Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem” (2 Samuel 23:24), and the roll is counted at its end: “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39). The Authorized Version keeps Harodite in Samuel and Harorite in Chronicles because that is what the two books have, and prints the alternative in the margin where the Hebrew allows it. The dictionary follows the same practice, naming Harorite inside this entry rather than making a second one.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Harodite, a native of Harod; the designation of two of David's mighty men at 2 Samuel 23:25.

Harodite is a gentilic, Hebrew Charodi, a man of Harod.

Harod is most likely the spring where Gideon's army was sifted.

It occurs twice, both in 2 Samuel 23:25.

It designates Shammah and Elika, two of David's thirty.

The Chronicles parallel gives the form Harorite at 1 Chronicles 11:27.

Modern Corruption

Parallel rolls that differ in a letter are made the ground of a general distrust of Scripture, where the difference is a known feature of the text and is printed openly.

expand to see more

Harodite in Samuel and Harorite in Chronicles differ by a single consonant, and such pairs are gathered by the thousand into arguments that the Old Testament cannot be trusted. The argument needs the pairs to matter, and they do not. No doctrine, no history and no promise turns on which letter stands in a gentilic; the two books agree that two men of one small town were in the company; and the translators printed the variant in the margin rather than choosing silently between them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that two men came out of Harod. If the town is Gideon's spring, then the place where an army was cut to three hundred afterwards sent two of the thirty-seven to David — and the God who had refused numbers there was pleased to name individuals here.
